implementation_notes: Thread::Queue is the standard-library realization: it implements all the locking for multi-producer, multi-consumer FIFO access, each pop removes exactly one element, and close() gives the channel an end-of-stream signal - push raises ClosedQueueError, pop returns nil on a drained closed queue while deq(true) raises ThreadError. Nothing has to be hand-written for an in-process channel, but its scope ends at the process and the GVL limits CPU parallelism, so production channels are usually broker-backed (Sidekiq/Resque on Redis, Bunny on RabbitMQ).
code_sketch:
q = Thread::Queue.new
workers = 2.times.map { Thread.new { while (job = q.pop) do handle(job) end } }
q.push(job)          # exactly one worker pops it
q.close              # pop of the drained queue returns nil, ending the loops
workers.each(&:join)
pitfalls: pop returns nil on a closed empty queue while deq(true) raises ThreadError; mixing the two styles hides lost work at shutdown.
Ruby threads share the GVL, so a CPU-bound consumer serializes regardless of worker count - scale out with processes (Sidekiq) instead.
A consumer blocked in pop pins its thread; without close or a sentinel value the process never exits.
